title: Australia news live: Economic hits driving voters towards One Nation, Labor boss says
body: One Nation’s rise in new heartland a warning to majors The rise of One Nation has seen heightened activity among local representatives of all political persuasions fighting for the limelight in the populist party’s new regional heartland, AAP reports. David Farley’s historic win for One Nation at the Farrer by-election in early-May sent shock waves through federal politics, especially the major parties. Observers now see One Nation’s management of the electorate - and the way the major parties respond - as a model on how the next federal election could be fought, amid a surge of support for the Pauline Hanson-led populists in national polls. Farley’s presence in Farrer’s major centres of Albury and Griffith, and his visits to the regional communities of the once safe Liberal electorate, have been noticed by politicians at a local level, according to Albury City mayor Kevin Mack. He says the increased scrutiny on the region has lit a fire under some local councillors: I’m seeing politicians going to the opening of envelopes. They seem to be going to things I’m not going to, which I didn’t know existed. They seem to be creating their own opportunities. The shift in approach from established politicians from major parties was a natural result when threatened by a rise from smaller ones, according to Australian National University political scientist Jill Sheppard. The great virtue of Australian politics is that we have stability, but the price of stability is the parties tend to get a bit lazy. For a normal voter who is just hoping life can feel a little bit better, that’s not always very satisfying. ... I suspect that there will be some kind of ripple effect from Albury. Coalition says PM wanted to ‘shut down debate’ at LNP national conference The Coalition says Anthony Albanese was desperate to shut down debate on contentious issues such as Aukus and Israel and Palestine at Labor’s national conference because he wanted to avoid exposing the “deep divisions” with the party. The party’s three-day conference ended on Saturday without any major fights after Ed Husic’s push to adopt a harder line on Israel collapsed amid resistance from factional powerbrokers. A proposed amendment from the party’s anti-war movement to abandon the Aukus pact also failed to reach the conference floor. The shadow defence minister, James Paterson, said it was “telling” that neither issue was debated at Labor’s peak policy-making forum. He said: I think it is very telling that rather than have the debate and win the debate, the prime minister and his government would prefer to shut down the debate. I think that shows what he knows. He knows that deep down there is deep divisions within the Labor Party on core national security interest issues, on core foreign policy issues, and on core defence policy issues. The prime minister is worried that he would be embarrassed on the floor of the conference if Aukus was allowed to be debated, or if Israel-Palestine was allowed to be debated, or indeed the US alliance was allowed to be debated. I think he shut that down because he was afraid about where it would go. Senior Labor sources denied actively attempting to block Husic’s resolution, arguing the former minister simply didn’t have any support. The Maritime Union of Australia initially agreed to second Husic’s motion before withdrawing support on Saturday morning, causing it to lapse. Some delegates who were sympathetic to Husic were reluctant to back the resolution because they didn’t want to potentially overshadow a display of unity arranged for the debate, when MPs Josh Burns, who is Jewish, and Basem Abdo, the son of Palestinian refugees, united in support of the government’s official position. Labor’s pro-Palestine wing did secure a win on Saturday with the party committing to strong controls and transparency around weapons export permits. Chris Bowen says Australia’s fuel supply ‘solid and secure’ The federal energy minister, Chris Bowen, has sought to assure Australians that fuel supply remains “solid and secure” as the drawn out Middle East conflict pushes global crude back above $US100 a barrel. Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Bowen said there was uncertainty about the situation in the Middle East: But one thing Australians can be certain about is that our fuel supply continues to be solid and secure. Bowen said as of Saturday, Australia had 42 days’ worth of petrol, 38 days’ worth of diesel and 32 days’ worth of jet fuel. There are 51 ships on route to Australia, with 3.1bn litres of fuel due to arrive in the next four weeks, he said. He said Australia’s fuel stock was 15% more than when the US and Israel first bombed Iran in February. Australia’s scaled-back extension of the fuel excise reduction is due to end on 2 August. Economists have warned that the end of the excise and higher global prices mean Australians face the prospect of petrol prices above $2 a litre over the coming weeks. Two more local birds with suspected deadly bird flu in South Australia South Australia has two more suspected cases of deadly H5 bird flu in local terns, marking a possible escalation in the disease’s presence in the state. On Saturday, the South Australian government said samples would be sent to CSIRO to verify whether the birds had the deadly H5N1 strain. Results are expected in the coming days. The two birds are greater crested terns, which members of the public found and reported. One was found dead near the Surf Life Saving Club at Semaphore in Adelaide and the other was found unwell at Robe and has since died. To date 17 cases of H5N1 have been confirmed nationally, with only one so far in a local bird - also a greater crested tern found at Robe Marina earlier this month. Federal agriculture minister Julie Collins said terns were known to mix with petrels and other migratory subantarctic species that had been found with bird flu. Collins said there was still no evidence of widespread local transmission of the disease: We have no evidence of any transmission in Australia in terms of the H5 bird flu at this point in time. We have no mass mortalities being recorded. We have no bird flu in our culture or agriculture systems, and the risk to human health remains low. Economic hits driving voters to One Nation: Labor boss Labor’s national secretary, Paul Erickson, says repeated economic hits are pushing voters to consider right wing parties like Pauline Hanson’s One Nation, warning major parties need to address these anxieties. Erickson is the campaign strategist behind Labor’s wins in 2022 and 2025 and is preparing to fight a reelection campaign for Anthony Albanese in about 18 months time. He told Sky: When we think about the last decade, one thing that has stood out is that every time workers and businesses felt like through the crisis, the latest crisis, and every time they’re picking themselves up off the floor, another big event comes along, another crisis. Whether it is war in Europe, war in the Middle East, a global inflation surge, all the way back to the pandemic, and that constant sense of every time you’re picking yourself up off the floor, another knock comes along, I think has led to a sense for people in the community of pessimism that, as progressives and as a centre-left party, we need to tackle and take on. But I think is at the core of this rise of the populist right all over the world. Good morning and happy Sunday, It’s Caitlin Cassidy here to guide you through today’s news. The prime minister has been accused by the Coalition of wanting to “shut down debate” at Labor’s national conference on issues like Aukus and Israel and Palestine at Labor’s national conference because he wanted to avoid exposing the “deep divisions” with the party. It comes as Ed Husic’s push for Labor to recognise claims of a genocide against Israel failed, prompting the backbencher to criticise the party’s culture under Anthony Albanese. South Australia has two more suspected cases of deadly H5 bird flu, marking a possible escalation in the disease’s presence in the state. Some 17 cases of H5N1 have now been confirmed nationally, with only one so far in a local bird. And the energy minister, Chris Bowen, has assured Australians that fuel supply remains “solid and secure” as the drawn out Middle East conflict pushes global crude back above $US100 a barrel. If you’d like to get in touch, I’m on caitlin.cassidy@theguardian.com. Let’s get into it!

title: Evacuated villagers in Cairngorms allowed home after wildfire threat lifts
summary: Scottish first minister thanks Nethy Bridge residents and aid workers after earlier requesting UK military aid to fight 10-day fire
body: Residents of Nethy Bridge have been told they can return to their homes after a large fire broke out in the Cairngorms national park. Supt Judy Hill of Police Scotland said: “Thanks to the efforts of fire crews, gamekeepers, contractors, partners and many others over the past 24 hours, there is no longer the immediate threat which prompted the evacuation of properties in Nethy Bridge. “We are grateful to the community for their support and understanding in what has been a period of concern and disruption.” Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, welcomed the news, saying: “Efforts to tackle the wildfire in the Cairngorms are in their 10th day, and changeable weather conditions have presented a range of challenges for those on the ground. I praise their resilience and tireless efforts to bring it under control. “With residents in Nethy Bridge now able to return to their homes, Police Scotland have lifted the major incident declaration. “I want to stress, however, that the Scottish government, the emergency services and all relevant authorities will continue to treat this wildfire, as has been the case since its onset, with the utmost seriousness and necessary resources until the last flames are out.” Earlier in the day Swinney had asked for military aid from the UK government as more than 500 firefighters alongside specialist wildfire appliances, all-terrain vehicles, helicopter water-bombing operations and partner agencies tackled the fire that had raged in the Cairngorms national park for the past 10 days and forced the evacuation of homes in the remote region. Residents of Nethy Bridge were taken to a dedicated respite centre at the Macdonald Aviemore hotel. Access roads were closed amid fears the fire was heading for the village. Just before 11pm on Saturday residents were told they could return home. Swinney had said earlier in the day that changing wind conditions had “intensified the pace of spread of the wildfire, adding that the Scottish fire and rescue service (SFRS) was focusing its resources on creating a firebreak. The wildfire, which broke out near the village of Glenmore on 15 July, led to residents and campsites being evacuated. It covered an area of about 6 sq km (2.3 sq miles) of heather and small trees at its height and its smoke drifted as far as Aberdeen, about 60 miles (97km) from where the fire started. Claire Montague, 65, a retired GP, and her family were evacuated from their home on Friday. She said: “We could see the smoke rising and when the wind changed direction we could see the flames – it was pretty scary and felt pretty close although it was still a few kilometres away. “We could see lots of smoke today when we popped back home, masses coming from a very large area. It is not contained by any means. “It was absolutely terrifying, nothing like I’ve felt before. The Dava Moor fire last summer was farther away from us. “Thankfully they have managed to put in a firebreak.” Montague added: “Where the fire started is the original area of the Caledonian forest, a desperately important ecosystem, which they were trying very hard to preserve and expand. “The whole land had to be bulldozed for the firebreak, which is desperately sad.” Senior emergency service officials said that firefighters “continue to work across a vast and challenging landscape alongside Forestry and Land Scotland, the Cairngorms national park authority, landowners, estate gamekeepers and emergency service partners. Their expertise, local knowledge and support have been instrumental in helping crews respond to this complex and dynamic incident.” On Saturday, the SFRA warned residents in Tomintoul – about 10 miles (16km) to the east of Nethy Bridge – to keep windows and doors closed because of the smoke from the wildfire.

title: Police investigate payments to Reform UK first revealed by the Guardian
summary: Scotland Yard is looking at two £250,000 donations to the party by Britain Means Business before the 2024 election
body: Payments to Reform UK first revealed by the Guardian are now being investigated by the Metropolitan police. The inquiry is scrutinising payments made to the party via a company controlled by its deputy leader, Richard Tice. Scotland Yard is looking at two donations of £250,000 made to the party by Britain Means Business in the weeks before the 2024 general election. The Guardian revealed earlier this month that Fiona Cottrell made a £1m transfer to Britain Means Business shortly before the donations were made. About half of the funds were then passed to the party. Cottrell’s son, George, is a convicted fraudster with close links to Reform’s leader, Nigel Farage. The Guardian reported earlier this month that Fiona and George Cottrell have been interviewed under criminal caution as part of the police investigation. In response to a query about the investigation from the BBC, Tice said: “This is the first I have heard of it – if true why are the Met police briefing the BBC before contacting interested parties? “Is the Met leadership now engaged in the widespread politically motivated smear campaign against Reform and its leaders?” Fiona Cottrell also made two donations directly to the party, each worth £250,000, in May 2024. These are also within the scope of the Metropolitan police investigation. Tice, who was elected to parliament after the poll, is the sole director of Britain Means Business. He has previously confirmed that his company received donations from Fiona Cottrell but described reports about the money as a “politically motivated smear campaign”. The Guardian told how the transfer from Fiona Cottrell to Britain Means Business was reported to the National Crime Agency by bankers via a suspicious activity report. Suspicious activity reports are not crime reports but exist to identify potential incidents of money laundering. The Guardian understands that neither the NCA nor bankers have been able to trace the source of the original £1m sent by Fiona Cottrell to Tice’s company. The NCA is seeking help from a foreign partner in its attempts to understand where the money originated. A Reform UK spokesperson said: “Reform takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations and always ensures that the Electoral Commission guidelines on donations, as set out in the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, are strictly followed, as has been the case with donations so far.” Fiona Cottrell did not respond to the Guardian’s attempts to contact her about the donations to Britain Means Business. When asked about the developments by the BBC on Saturday evening, the Metropolitan police repeated a statement issued earlier this month. “An investigation was launched in February 2025 after a referral was made to the Metropolitan police by the Electoral Commission relating to donations made to a political party ahead of the 2024 UK general election,” the force said. “Detectives from the Met’s special enquiry team are investigating alleged offences under section 61 of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000. “Early investigative advice has been sought from the Crown Prosecution Service and two people have so far been interviewed under caution. No arrests have been made. “An offence under this section is not one that the Electoral Commission can investigate and, as such, it is a matter for the police.”

title: More than 1 million children lost access to food benefits after Trump bill passed
summary: Analysis finds more than 4 million Americans lost Snap benefits, or food stamps, from July 2025 to March 2026
body: More than a million children across the US have lost access to Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (Snap) food benefits since Congress approved the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025, according to a new report from the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities (CBPP). The analysis found that more than 4 millions Americans were removed from Snap from July 2025 to March 2026, marking a significant decline in participation in the federal food assistance program. Arizona recorded the largest drop in enrollment after the bill became law. The legislation tightened eligibility rules for food assistance and increased state screening requirements. State data through May shows that more than 450,000 Arizonans have come off Snap, cutting overall participation within the state in half. According to the CBPP analysis, children make up a significant portion of those losing benefits, with more than 1 million children across the 19 states studied no longer receiving Snap assistance. In Louisiana, nearly one in four children receiving Snap benefits lost assistance. Massachusetts and Texas each saw close to one-fifth of children enrolled in the program removed from Snap. The report comes as participation in the program continues to fall nationwide following major reductions to the federal food assistance program under the Trump administration. Snap, commonly referred to as food stamps, provides monthly benefits to low-income and no-income households to help pay for groceries and remains the country’s largest food assistance program. The report says the steep decline in participation is likely tied in large part to the 2025 Republican reconciliation law, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which shifted a substantial share of Snap benefit costs to states based on their payment error rates. The CBPP warned that the situation would continue to deteriorate unless Congress intervenes. “Without immediate congressional action to delay this cost shift for all states, the unfolding emergency will only worsen as more children are cut off from the food assistance their families need to afford nutritious food,” the CBPP said. Representative Ilhan Omar, a progressive Democrat from Minnesota, pointed to the outcomes during a speech on the House floor earlier this month. Omar had introduced an amendment aimed at reversing the Snap cuts, but the proposal was rejected by the Republican majority. The latest figures also prompted action from the US Conference of Mayors. On Monday, the nonpartisan organization representing cities with populations of at least 30,000 sent a letter to the Senate signed by more than 200 mayors calling for lawmakers to reverse the Snap cuts amid the US’s “deepening food security crisis”. “Snap remains the nation’s most effective and efficient anti-hunger program. It reduces poverty, supports local economies, and provides an automatic stabilizer during economic downturns,” the letter said. “Hunger is not a partisan issue, and efforts to address food insecurity should rise above political divisions.”

title: Troy Jackson secures Democratic nomination for Maine Senate seat after chaotic primary race
summary: Progressive former state senate president gains nomination after Graham Platner dropped out over sexual assault allegations
body: In a race defined by scandal, withdrawals and a frantic hunt for a replacement candidate, Maine Democrats hit reset on their chaotic Senate primary on Saturday as Troy Jackson officially secured the party’s nomination. He took the stage at the Cross Insurance Center in Bangor to rapturous applause, a standing ovation and Noah Kahan’s Northern Attitude blaring over the speakers. “This is the absolute honor of my life,” Jackson said. “If you’ve ever been ignored, underestimated, pushed around or told that you have to wait your turn while the rich cut the line, I’m asking you to stand with us in this campaign.” Jackson’s win amounted to a coronation for the progressive fifth‑generation logger and former state senate president, who faced no real opposition at the special convention after every major rival stepped aside. Their exits cleared the path for Jackson to replace Graham Platner, the oysterman and marine veteran who ended his campaign amid mounting controversies that culminated in a sexual assault allegation he has denied. Platner dropped out days after Politico reported that a woman he dated five years ago said he forced her to have sex despite repeated objections. His withdrawal triggered a breakneck scramble inside the Maine Democratic party to devise a process for selecting a new nominee before the state’s 27 July deadline to select a replacement for the general‑election ballot. “I know many of you poured your hearts into building this movement way before I ever entered this race,” Jackson said on Saturday before the official vote. “But the hope that you built never belonged to anyone campaigning. It belongs to every Mainer who knows that healthcare is a human right, belongs to every worker fighting for a union, a living wage and a dignified environment.” Jackson, who finished third in the ranked‑choice gubernatorial primary, won the snap convention by a vote of 566-5 on Saturday. But his victory was all but assured once a majority of Mainers who won county‑level delegate elections last weekend pledged to back him before the convention. The remaining delegates come from the state party committee. By Sunday, as Jackson’s nomination became inevitable, all of his major challengers bowed out of the hastily assembled contest. That included fellow gubernatorial contenders – former Maine CDC director Nirav Shah and the Maine secretary of state, Shenna Bellows – as well as Jordan Wood, the former congressional candidate who ran unsuccessfully in the Democratic primary for Maine’s second district. “The easy solution”, said the Maine Democratic party chair, Charlie Dingman, would be to let the state committee select the new nominee. “Instead, we responded to the growing grassroots movement in our state to build power for ordinary working people,” he said. However, some Democratic voters said the convention process was still not representative of the more than 200,000 voters who turned out in the primary to elect Platner in June. Jackson will now face the five‑term Republican incumbent, Susan Collins, in one of the most closely watched races of the midterm cycle – for a seat Democrats view as central to their audacious plan to retake the Senate. They need four pickups nationwide in November, and Maine is integral to that strategy. Collins is also the only Republican in the upper chamber seeking re-election in a state that Kamala Harris won in 2024. “For 30 years, she’s told us that she’s ‘concerned’. But look, concern is not courage,” Jackson said on Saturday, as supporters waved “Retire Susan” placards in the audience. “What she says in Maine does not erase what she does down in Washington.” Preliminary polling from the University of New Hampshire shows Jackson with a slight edge over Collins, a moderate GOP senator who has been politically untouchable for the past three decades. And while Jackson is well-known in Maine political circles, his nascent campaign will have to accelerate quickly to match Collins’s fundraising lead and the momentum Platner built after months of statewide travel, town halls and a grassroots surge strong enough to force the term‑limited governor, Janet Mills, out of the Democratic primary in April. Jackson, who began his political career as a Republican and once opposed abortion and gay marriage, is now staunchly progressive and campaigned alongside Platner’s economic‑populist platform, even earning Platner’s endorsement during his own unsuccessful run for governor. Both points are likely to feature prominently in the efforts by Collins and conservative groups to undermine his political acumen in the months ahead. Shortly after Platner exited the race, Jackson tried to distance himself from the turmoil – telling MS Now that Platner assured him there was “nothing in his past that I had to worry about”. “He lied to me. And he lied to a lot of us,” Jackson said in an interview after Platner posted an 11‑minute video announcing his withdrawal. In Bangor on Saturday, the new nominee insisted the chaos that has consumed the Democratic race was in the rearview mirror without naming Platner. “Today we turn the page. Today this becomes a general election campaign, and today we begin the work of defeating Susan Collins in November,” Jackson said. A number of delegates said that Jackson’s proximity to Platner’s messaging shouldn’t be off-putting. “It never was about the person, but about the policies,” said Lydia Stone, 31, who lives in North Yarmouth and works for a company that sells forestry supplies. “I think what Graham said he was, I think Troy Jackson actually is.” Many people in Bangor noted that it was crucial for Jackson to be meeting voters as much as possible in the 101 days until the election. “It’s going to be difficult because there’s a short window window of time, but I would say to get out there as much as he can into especially those rural communities like where he’s from, and actually be there,” said Lisa Marin, 69, who lives in Jonesport and chairs the Washington county Democratic committee. Marin added: “That was one of the things in the Platner campaign that I think was really helpful for Graham – he was out there and really meeting people where they are. And I know Troy wants to do that, and as much as he can, I feel like that’s what he needs to do.”

title: France and Spain race to control wildfires as more than 250,000 evacuated – as it happened
summary: Meanwhile, in the UK, a blaze in the Cairngorms national park has been described as ‘very serious’ by Scotland’s first minister
body: Firefighters across France and Spain continue to battle wildfires that have displaced almost 270,000 people. A ‌man has died in a ‌wildfire near the Spanish city of Valencia, the country’s ⁠interior ⁠ministry said. The victim was ‌found in a car ⁠in a ravine in the town of Manises, west of the city. In France, 197,000 people have been evacuated near Bordeaux, including in the suburbs of the city. The French armed forces significantly expanded its military response to the major wildfires in the south-west, deploying 1,500 soldiers to support firefighters, assist with evacuations and provide medical care, transport, accommodation, and logistical support. The armed forces are also supplying specialist equipment, including bulldozers, helicopters, drones, and A400M military aircraft equipped for aerial firefighting, to help contain the fires and support the wider emergency response. The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, convened new government crisis meeting later on the wildfires in south-west France, his office announced. The Spanish interior ministry said a total of 70,000 people have been evacuated from villages west of Madrid. Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said the wildfire situation near Madrid remained “complex” as he visited affected areas. “We don’t know how the wind will develop, even though temperatures have dropped,” he said. The first minister of Scotland has asked for military aid from the UK government as more than 500 firefighters continue to tackle a firewhich has raged in the Cairngorms national park for the past 11 days and forced the evacuation of homes in the remote region. More than 400 emergency personnel are working to contain the wildfire to the west of the Spanish capital, Madrid’s emergency agency ASEM112 said, in addition to 50 ground and 12 aerial units such as fire engines and helicopters. Rodika, 60, from the small town of Fresnedillas de La Oliva near Madrid, told Reuters she was evacuated around 30 minutes away. “I saw clouds of smoke rising into the sky. That’s when I realized something was happening. “I think we all panicked. Then we received the message telling us to get ready, take whatever valuables we could, whatever was most important. I took my cat, and we left.” The evacuation was similar for Julio, 41, in the nearby town of Navalgamella. “Neighbours were shouting, the police were shouting, everything was happening at once. We packed the essentials: two or three changes of clothes, my medication in my case, some cash, and we left,” he said. A ‌man has died in a ‌wildfire near the Spanish city of Valencia, the country’s ⁠interior ⁠ministry said. The victim was ‌found in a car ⁠in a ravine in the town of Manises, west of the city. Sunday’s stage of the Tour de France has been shortened to 89km from the original 133km to allow security personnel to be redeployed to tackle wildfires near Bordeaux, organisers and police said. Spain’s interior ministry said residents in the town of San Martin de Valdeiglesias and the village of Valdemaqueda, near Madrid, should stay indoors. More than 28,000 people are already under lockdown in the autonomous region of Madrid and the Avila municipality, the ministry added. Unrestrained wildfires in Spain and France have forced more than 250,000 people to flee, authorities from both countries have said, as they struggle to contain the blazes. About 70,000 people were evacuated from central Spain, while 197,000 people fled in France, including tens of thousands from the wine region city of Bordeaux. Spain declared a national emergency over the fires, the first time the country has ever done so over a wildfire. Hundreds of firefighters have worked to contain the blazes, which have been fuelled by persistent heatwaves and the climate crisis, but were still unable to stop their advance. In Spain, high winds were exacerbating the fires, and two of the three merged on Friday. France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said a huge military cargo plane, the Airbus A400M Atlas, was being deployed to join 18 other aircraft in the “long and very difficult” battle against wildfires in the Gironde region of south-western France. The French armed forces have significantly expanded its military response to the major wildfires in the south-west, deploying 1,500 soldiers to support firefighters, assist with evacuations and provide medical care, transport, accommodation, and logistical support. The armed forces are also supplying specialist equipment, including bulldozers, helicopters, drones, and A400M military aircraft equipped for aerial firefighting, to help contain the fires and support the wider emergency response. In a post on X, Catherine Vautrin, the minister of the armed forces who attended an emergency meeting at the army headquarters, said: “Our forces are engaged on the ground in support of the internal security forces and civil security forces as part of the state’s response to a sudden, major, and unprecedented crisis, to protect people, property, and businesses.” Here’s a video showing the extent of the devastation wrought on Spain and France as firefighters continue to battle the wildfires: The Spanish civil guard has warned misinformation and images not related to the wildfires in the Madrid and Ávila regions were circulating online, as it advised people to follow official channels and media outlets for information. It said the following areas were being evacuated: Madrid: Las Rozas de Puerto Real, Cadalso de los Vidrios, Cenicientos and the Entrepinos estate. Ávila: La Adrada, Piedralaves, Sotillo de la Adrada, Casillas and Santa María del Tiétar, la Iglesuela and Arenas de San Pedro. The French newspaper Le Monde has noted that more than 32,000 hectares (79,000 acres) of land have burned in Gironde, an area equivalent to three times the size of Paris. Some pictures on the newswires from Lacanau, in the Gironde region of south-west France, where firefighters and volunteers are trying to contain the wildfire: Back in Scotland, a community leader in the Highlands village of Nethy Bridge has described the scenes of a wildfire in Cairngorms national park which has been burning for 11 days. “Apocalyptic is the word for the pall of smoke that was on the go yesterday,” Sandy McCook told PA. McCook said there was a major increase in firefighting units in and around the village, plus multiple wildfire response units. “I think a lot of people are running on adrenaline,” he said. “A lot of people are upset, angry and frustrated at the ongoing situation because the Scottish government said a week ago [on Wednesday] that they had enough resources to deal with it, and they said on Thursday that the fire was contained. “My argument with that is, if you said the fire was contained and you had enough resources last Wednesday and Thursday, why are we still fighting it 10 days later and it’s still running out of control? It is still not controlled in any way shape or form.” The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, has issued a message of solidarity with France and Spain, saying more help from the EU is on the way to aid firefighting missions. In a post on X, she said: Europe stands alongside France and Spain in the face of the devastating wildfires ravaging them. 5 planes and 2 helicopters from the rescEU fleet are now deployed in France. And 4 planes are arriving in Spain today. Copernicus is also providing emergency mapping to support the response in both countries. My thoughts are with the firefighters who bravely battle the flames and with all those evacuated.” The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, will convene a new government crisis meeting later this afternoon on the wildfires in south-west France, his office announced. It comes after a meeting yesterday resulted in the dispatch of more troops and a military water-dumping aircraft to the fire-hit region near Bordeaux. More from Cairngorms in Scotland, where people in the village of Nethy Bridge were told to evacuate as a precaution last night as the situation around the wildfire in the nearby national park deteriorated. The Press Association spoke to villager Richard Eccles and his wife, Patricia, who have lived in Nethy Bridge for 33 years. They told the news agency that police came to their house at around 10pm and presented them with three options – they could either stay, seek accommodation with friends or family elsewhere or go to emergency accommodation at the Macdonald hotel in Aviemore about 10 miles away. They said they decided to stay unless the fire gets considerably closer, which most residents in the village appear to have done. Mr Eccles said: “We’ve got a camper van and we’re all ready and set to go at a moment’s notice.” He continued: “If it gets smoky, we’ll go.” He said the Scottish government’s response had been “poor” and a major incident should have been declared earlier, with military assistance brought in to tackle the fire before it spread. Mr Eccles said: “It’s a bit like closing the stable door now that the horse has bolted.” The Spanish government has ordered the entire Tiétar Valley in the province of Ávila to evacuate, affecting 30,000 people, the government delegate in Madrid, Francisco Martín, said. He added that there were also evacuation orders in the towns of Rozas de Puerto Real and Cadalso de los Vidrios west of Madrid. If you’re just joining us, here are the day’s main developments: Firefighters across France and Spain continue to battle wildfires that have displaced almost 270,000 people. In France, 197,000 people have been evacuated near Bordeaux, including in the suburbs of the city. title: ‘It felt like the end of the world’: Spanish wildfire evacuees tell of their narrow escapes
summary: The people of Robledo near Madrid witnessed unearthly scenes of devastation as their town was consumed by fire
body: When David Olivares went to bed on Thursday night, tired from a four-hour motorbike ride, the fire creeping towards his home town of Robledo de Chavela seemed a distant menace. He woke up the next day, saw the white smoke behind the mountains and decided the threat to Robledo, which lies 30 miles (50km) west of Madrid, had probably receded. The feeling of idle security would not last long. A second look at the horizon revealed the white smoke was beginning to give way to black. “Then I saw the fire at the top of the mountain,” said the 27-year-old as he ate a sandwich in the leisure centre to which he had been evacuated in Las Rozas, a municipality on the north-western outskirts of the Spanish capital. “It started to spread down the mountain and then I got the emergency alert on my phone at about 5.30pm, telling us we had to leave.” Even so, he wasn’t unduly panicked. “I thought to myself, come on, it’s 2026 – the firefighters will get it under control with all their drones and planes,” he said. “But that wasn’t the case.” Just as his mother told him they needed to leave, Olivares looked up at the sky, which had also begun to change. “It turned orange and looked very apocalyptic,” he said. “Then there was black smoke in Robledo and you could see the fire. People were shouting – a kid was screaming to his dad: ‘Let’s go now’ – and there were cars and people everywhere. It felt like the end of the world. We grabbed our three cats, got in the car and left.” María Rosa Marín, a fellow evacuee from the nearby town of Valdemaqueda, nodded along at the recollection. “The sun was so strange; you could hardly see it. It looked like something from the Bible,” she said. On a cushion next to her lay her dog, Jeffery, who dozed on, blissfully unconcerned at finding himself so far from home and under such dramatic circumstances. Marín, Olivares and 300 or so other people who were evacuated from Robleda and the surrounding towns had spent the night in the sports centre in Las Rozas, where council workers were preparing stacks of ham sandwiches and local police officers were lugging in huge bottles of water. They are just a few of the 87,000 people who have been evacuated or ordered to lock down as central Spain battles huge wildfires that scientists say are being fuelled by climate breakdown and plentiful dry vegetation on a continent that is heating at about twice the global average rate. David Santos, Las Rozas’s councillor for safety and emergencies, said people had been arriving at the centre since 1pm on Friday. “They’re pretty worried and pretty anxious,” he said. “We’re talking about people who’ve been evacuated from their homes and their home towns and don’t know when they’ll be able to return. On top of that, they don’t know whether their homes will be intact, so they’re living in a state of uncertainty.” Santos said three emergency psychologists were on hand at the centre to help people, as well as paramedics and a doctor. For the young, games and books were available on the top floor of the sports centre and there were plans to screen a film on Sunday. The councillor, who has overseen the town’s response to everything from the heavy snowfall of Storm Filomena five years ago to the Covid pandemic and the hosting of an large influx of Ukrainian refugees, said nothing quite compared with the blaze that Madrid’s regional president has described as “the worst wildfire in our region’s history”. José Celaya, another evacuee from Robledo, sat at a nearby communal table, working his way through another of the many ham sandwiches. The 61-year-old, who had arrived at the sports centre late on Friday night with his wife, two children, sister-in-law and mother-in-law, shook his head at the suggestion that Spain’s wildfires were becoming more frequent because of climate breakdown. He laid the blame squarely at the door of successive governments, which had turned their backs on the huge rural and semi-rural swathes of the country. “I think it’s complete negligence, a totally misguided policy by the governments – and I don’t care which government is in power,” he said. “Their policies have nothing to do with how we used to look after the hills: there’s no livestock to graze them now and no one to clear all the vegetation. They don’t let people gather firewood, which, after all, is flammable material.” Still, he said, indignation and frustration would serve no purpose at the moment. And besides, he added, all the staff and volunteers at the sports centre had been amazing. “There’s no point getting wound up, because getting angry isn’t going to solve anything,” said Celaya. “Everyone just has to cope as best they can. Everything depends on the weather now – on how windy it is and on which way the wind blows.”

title: More than 250,000 people flee wildfires in France and Spain
summary: Hundreds of firefighters battle blazes as strong winds drive fires towards Bordeaux and smoke prompts health warnings in Madrid
body: Unrestrained wildfires in Spain and France have forced more than 250,000 people to flee, authorities from both countries have said, as they struggle to contain the blazes. About 70,000 people were evacuated from central Spain, while 197,000 people fled in France, including tens of thousands from the wine region city of Bordeaux. Spain declared a national emergency, the first time the country has ever done so over a wildfire. France’s evacuations constituted “probably” the biggest peacetime evacuation the country has ever seen, its interior minister said. Hundreds of firefighters have worked to contain the blazes, which have been fuelled by persistent heatwaves and the climate crisis, but were still unable to stop their advance. In Spain, high winds were exacerbating the fires, and two of the three blazes merged on Friday. France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said a huge military cargo plane, the Airbus A400M Atlas, was being deployed to join 18 other aircraft in the “long and very difficult” battle against wildfires in the Gironde region of south-western France. The French government has called in the military to help, deploying 1,500 soldiers, and has rushed 1.5m face masks to help protect people from smoke inhalation. Fire crews have also been digging trenches, as well as using retardants, as winds were forecast to push the fires closer to Bordeaux. Wildfires were reported to be about 20 miles west of the city. The French government ordered people in the path of the fire to evacuate, including those in Bordeaux’s western suburbs. Police went door to door to tell people to leave, with scenes of panic unfolding as residents fled their homes under a smoke-darkened sky. The Gironde regional prefect, Sophie Brocas, said on Friday that strong winds were driving the fire towards the Bordeaux metro area and that it had grown to “an unprecedented magnitude”. Officials said the sudden blazes caught residents and authorities off guard. Some people in France had to flee by boat when the flames headed towards coastal towns. The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the fire in Gironde was so strong that it had begun generating its own winds. “The fires that are hitting our country have reached a level that has never been seen before,” he wrote on X. “Our priority is clear: protecting human lives.” He urged people to obey evacuation orders “without delay”. The Spanish health minister instructed people in Madrid not to go outside over concern of the poor air quality. “Avoid physical activity and staying outdoors. If you go outdoors and there is smoke or ash, use a mask,” Monica Garcia said on X. On Saturday evening, Spain’s interior ministry said a man had died in a fire in Manises, in Valencia. He had been found in a car in a ravine, officials said. The fire was a separate incident from the major blazes raging west of Madrid, which have so far not caused any reported deaths. The long, back-to-back heatwaves in Europe have dried forests out, turning them into tinder for wildfires. Fires had already consumed 130,000 hectares (320,000 acres) of forest this year in Spain, about a third higher than the country’s annual average, Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said on Saturday. In France, fires burned down more than 98,000 hectares, which France’s interior minister said was a “historic record”. Scientists say climate breakdown is triggering more frequent and more extreme weather events, evaporating soils and waterways, fuelling wildfires and leading to thousands of excess deaths. Europe is heating at about twice the global average rate. Sánchez said that cooler weather on Saturday gave a “window of opportunity” for firefighters to help contain the blazes. “We are going to have some complex hours ahead because, although the temperatures have gone down, we do not know exactly how the wind will develop, how strong it will be,” he added. Other European countries were helping both countries fight the blazes, with Croatia, the Czech Republic, Greece, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal and Slovakia sending aid and water-dumping aircraft to France and Spain. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, promised more help was on the way. “Europe stands alongside France and Spain in the face of the devastating wildfires ravaging them. Five planes and two helicopters from the rescue fleet are now deployed in France and four planes are arriving in Spain today,” she said on X.

title: New North Sea oil drilling faces delay after gear accidentally dropped in sea
summary: Exclusive: Blunder at Rosebank, UK’s biggest undeveloped oilfield, comes as government considers granting licence
body: Production at Britain’s biggest undeveloped oil and gasfield could be delayed for months after equipment from a rig was accidentally dropped in the North Sea, the Guardian can reveal. Andy Burnham’s new government is under pressure from the fossil fuel industry to allow oil to be retrieved from the Rosebank site despite opposition from climate campaigners and some Labour MPs. Rosebank, located about 80 miles north-west of Shetland, was believed to be ready to generate oil before the end of the year, pending ministerial approval. Adura, the company responsible for Rosebank, now says it anticipates this will happen at some point in 2027. The field is projected to produce 300m barrels of oil over its 25-year lifespan, according to industry estimates. Some MPs believe enhanced domestic production of oil and gas would help tackle the cost of living, a central focus of the new prime minister, by improving energy security amid global instability, while green campaigners believe the impact on the UK economy of exploiting the fields would be minimal. However, delays at Rosebank mean production at the field will be unlikely to affect the UK’s energy supply over the winter months. Licences for Rosebank and another site, Jackdaw, were granted under the Conservatives but operations were paused after a court challenge by environmental groups. The new energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is expected to make a decision on the fields’ future after consultations regarding their emissions conclude in August. Earlier this week, Adura told the BBC that the Jackdaw site, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen, could produce gas as early as October. However, preparations for oil production at Rosebank have been hindered by the rig incident, which occurred on 18 April. No workers were hurt, but two central pieces of drilling equipment, including a safety valve, were dropped 1,100 metres on to the seabed. The platform, hired by Adura from Norwegian company Odfjell Drilling, was taken to a shipyard in Bergen for repairs. It is now back at Rosebank but not yet operational. Odfjell Drilling said in internal documentation that the rig could be out of action for up to four months. The Guardian understands this means that some oil wells will be completed significantly behind schedule. Burnham is facing calls from trade unions and opposition parties to ramp up North Sea production. Some Labour MPs say the oil and gas industry, centred around Aberdeen, could face collapse without new investment. Sally Jameson, a Cabinet Office minister, has also argued that more domestic production of oil and gas would give Britain greater control over the cost of energy. Others fear it would have no real impact on bills, while wreaking untold damage on the climate. Mike Reader, part of the Labour Environment Campaign, said there was no evidence new drilling would save jobs in the long term. The Guardian revealed that only 27 direct full-time jobs would be created by Jackdaw, one of the biggest gasfields remaining in the North Sea, according to an environmental impact assessment filed publicly by Adura. Ed Miliband, the new foreign secretary, previously described the Rosebank proposals as “climate vandalism” when Labour was in opposition. However, in recent weeks talks are believed to have taken place on how to allow new drilling without breaching Labour’s 2024 manifesto commitments, in which it pledged not to issue new licences but honour existing ones. Several environmental groups are understood to be considering whether they would have grounds to take legal action regarding any government decision to allow new drilling. Angeliki Papantoniou, a lecturer in environmental law at the University of Hull, said that, while a fresh challenge would be a “long shot”, it would be most likely to succeed if based on “substantive environmental matters” such as the disruption of ecosystems, pollution and potential health impacts. “It could be argued that those developments cannot reasonably be ignored when taking a decision with likely high environmental effects,” she said. “In theory, it could be hard for [Fahnbulleh] to claim that [the government] took all necessary precautionary measures without detailed risk assessments on the effects of drilling on the marine environment, climate and human health.” Areeba Hamid, co-executive director of Greenpeace, which challenged the original decision to grant licences, said approval for the fields would make “zero difference” to energy bills and generate few jobs. “Despite these meagre benefits, we would be prolonging a polluting industry that’s fuelling heatwaves while sending a disastrous signal to our international allies,” she said. Odfjell Drilling declined to comment. Adura did not respond to a request for comment.

title: Eight family members found dead in Michigan fire, some with gunshot wounds
summary: Firefighters responded to an emergency call and found the bodies, six of which were those of children
body: A devastating tragedy has unfolded in Michigan after emergency crews responding to a house fire found eight members of the same family, including six children, dead. At least some of the dead inside the home had gunshot wounds. Deputies with the Ottawa county sheriff’s office and firefighters from the Grand Haven fire department were dispatched at about 11.40am local time on Friday to a residence on Riverside Trail in Grand Haven Township. Once crews entered the smoke-filled home to extinguish the fire, they made the grim discovery. “Units made entry inside to battle the fire because there was smoke showing from the residence. When they got inside, they noticed that there were several people deceased inside the home,” Capt Jacob Sparks said at a press conference. “Some of the victims did have gunshot wounds to their bodies.” Officials confirmed the victims were two adults and six children between the ages of five and 15. Their identities have not yet been released. Autopsies are scheduled to be completed over the weekend, according to ABC News, as investigators continue working to determine exactly what happened. Authorities said they are not currently looking for any suspects from outside the home, though Sparks stressed the investigation is ongoing. “I don’t want to jump to any conclusions at this point,” he said. Investigators with the Michigan state police’s arson team have joined the investigation. Officials believe the fire originated inside the residence, but the exact cause and point of origin have not yet been determined. The home is located in Grand Haven Township, just outside the city of Grand Haven and about 20 miles (32km) south of Muskegon, Michigan. According to the Ottawa county sheriff’s office, first responders arrived at a home shortly before noon after receiving reports of a fire and smoke. Firefighters discovered all eight victims after entering the residence to battle the flames. The investigation remains active, and authorities said additional information is expected after the victims’ autopsies are completed.

title: Wealthy gen Xers stand in the way of a Burnham tax on the super-rich
summary: If Andy Burnham wants to make the system fairer he will need to upset the professional classes with a land value tax
body: The professional classes act like a Praetorian Guard for the super-rich. Having acquired some of the trappings of being rich, they defend the privileges of wealth – land, property and pensions. They do this as if they – company managers, lawyers, doctors, judges, senior civil servants, architects and chartered this and thats – were the main beneficiaries. Crucially, tax is a hill that many upper middle-income gen Xers and baby boomers are prepared to die on. That is, they will die at some point, and want to take as much money with them, whether as a sign of success, to secure their families financial security or to give to charity. Whatever the reason, they definitely don’t want democratically elected bodies – national or local – to have the money. It is true they pay a much higher proportion of the government’s tax receipts than they did 15 years ago, hence their reluctance to pay any more. It is an understandable stance, except that the tax system they now defend is one that is so complex and riddled with distorting incentives that it is slowly destroying the economy. And it allows the super-rich to escape almost all obligations to support the society that gave them huge wealth in the first place. The professional classes appear to care little that their defence of the current tax system undermines the incentive for work, and especially to work as a salaried employee, or that the current tax system deters business investment. They have calculated that their high level of wealth will be enough to cash out, hopefully as part of an early retirement package, live on the proceeds for the rest of their days and hand on the surplus to their favoured recipients. It might seem unfair to pick on a particular group, but wealthy gen Xers – those born from 1965 to 1980 (making them 46 to 61 years old) – and baby boomers born after the war and before the 1960s really began to swing, are the people in charge of pretty much everything; and, as such, are a powerful lobby against changes to the tax system. Sparks are about to fly because one of the battlegrounds in Andy Burnham’s first months in office will be how to raise funds to support a wide array of measures he hopes will improve living standards. The new prime minister’s ability to borrow more funds will be limited, leaving his advisers with little option but to raise more tax. Taxing the rich will fit with his pledge to make the government “more Labour” to please the left flank of his party, which still flexes its considerable muscle despite Jeremy Corbyn’s expulsion. The tax change that would do more for the economy and would introduce a huge dose of fairness into the system would be a land value tax (LVT). Anyone who wants to read more about how we could ditch council tax and stamp duty – the two main taxes on property – in favour of an annual tax on the value of land can see the latest discussion paper by Dan Neidle’s Tax Policy Associates. It replaces the £45.2bn raised by council tax and the £11.5bn from stamp duty with a flat LVT rate of 1.28%. Under the Neidle scheme, LVT raises £56.7bn. By his calculation, about 70% of homes pay less than their current council tax. These homes are mostly outside London and the south-east. The super-rich would be unable to dodge the tax because they cannot shift the land they own overseas. Economists are almost uniformly in favour. One of the leading proponents, Fred Harrison, has written about how LVT was discussed in the highest circles during the early 19th century, just as wealth was being accumulated and largely untaxed, but defeated by lobbying from the newly minted professional classes. Burnham has spoken in favour of a land tax, and he could phase in a scheme that replaces council tax and stamp duty, setting England, and possibly the other countries of the UK if they follow suit, in an exciting new direction towards land being used more productively and not as a store of wealth. In the meantime, he needs extra cash. There are people close to the prime minister lobbying for a rise in capital gains tax (CGT) to match the thresholds for income tax. This would discourage taxpayers from accumulating wealth at the expense of income, which has been a trend for the last 40 years. Another, possibly complementary idea, focuses on those families with more than £100m in assets, which studies have shown can pay as little as zero tax and have an average tax rate at least half that paid by the bottom 80% of households. These wealthy families can sidestep CGT because they are so rich they do not need to sell assets and trigger a much higher CGT payout. These initiatives could raise £10bn-plus each. A tax commission that reported almost six years ago recommended a one-off wealth tax that raised more than £300bn. Tackling the issue will not be for the faint-hearted. As long as the professional classes remain determined to protect their privileges and luck from 40 years of pension and property accumulation at the expense of economic growth, Burnham’s resolve will be tested.

title: Former top US food safety official says US mismanagement of cyclospora is approaching ‘a catastrophic level’
summary: Frank Yiannas, formerly of the FDA, calls for an independent review of federal response to illness causing explosive diarrhea
body: Donald Trump’s former top food safety official has accused the administration of a near “catastrophic” mismanagement of the cyclospora outbreak that has sickened thousands of people in the US. There should be an independent review of the federal government’s response to the rash of illnesses caused by the spread of a parasite found on raw produce, according to Frank Yiannas, who was deputy commissioner for food policy at the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) across the presidencies of both Trump and Joe Biden from 2018 to 2023. “This one deserves a lot of questions, and it is starting to approach a catastrophic level in terms of how mismanaged it’s been on multiple fronts,” Yiannas told Politico. Yiannas said there has been widespread public confusion about cyclosporiasis, an intestinal illness caused by the microscopic parasite Cyclospora cayetanensis, also known as cyclospora, that can cause explosive diarrhea. This has been compounded by a “lack of strong federal leadership” and mixed messages from federal agencies, he added. The chaotic response to cyclospora, which has sickened more than 4,000 people in the US with thousands more thought to have also been affected, has been highlighted by the attempts to identify and halt the source of the outbreak. The FDA identified lettuce from Taylor Farms, a supplier to Taco Bell, as being linked to the outbreak, only to then backtrack. Taylor Farms has said that the FDA apologized to the company for this, a claim that the FDA has denied. The federal food regulator still maintains there is strong evidence connecting Taylor Farms, which has recalled its lettuce, to the outbreak. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, said last week the outbreak was “under control”, even as the FDA expanded its investigation into 7,400 potential cases across nine states. “They just went too fast and they made a mistake,” Yiannas said of the FDA. “They should share more about how and why it happened and what they’ll do to prevent it in the future.” A review of the government’s response should have congressional oversight or be done via an independent inspector, Yiannas said. The FDA has not immediately responded to this call for an investigation of its actions.

title: India’s education minister resigns in victory for Cockroach youth movement protests
summary: Dharmendra Pradhan steps down after demonstrations over exam leak scandal, prompting celebrations among thousands of protesters
body: India’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, has resigned after a week of mass demonstrations, handing a major victory to a new youth movement that has posed an unprecedented challenge to Narendra Modi’s government. In a statement on Saturday afternoon, Pradhan said he had submitted his letter of resignation to the prime minister after student pressure. “Considering the situation that has arisen at Jantar Mantar and ‌across the country, so that anti-national forces do not take advantage of this situation … I have sent my resignation letter to the prime minister,” Pradhan wrote in a social media post. He said he had been “saddened by what unfolded over the last 10 days”, but added: “I deeply respect the aspirations, feelings, and legitimate expectations ‌of the country’s youth.” During his 12 years in power, Modi has cultivated a strongman image and has maintained his ministers are not accountable to public pressure. This was the first time a mass uprising had forced one of his most loyal ministers to resign. The protests were organised by a newly formed youth political movement, the Cockroach Janata party (CJP), which has escalated into a nationwide uprising of youth dissent this week. The core demand of the CJP and its supporters was the resignation of Pradhan over an exam leak scandal that has devastated the lives of millions of students and led to more than a dozen students taking their own lives. The refusal by Modi to sack his minister over the scandal was widely seen as symbolic of the alleged lack of accountability of the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and its repeated failure to address the issues faced by young people, particularly in the country’s flawed education system. CJP organisers confirmed they had called off their demonstration after Pradhan’s resignation and a meeting with senior BJP ministers on Saturday afternoon. In a speech to the crowds gathered at the Delhi Jantar Mantar protest site, CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, saluted the “courage” of students who had turned out in huge numbers, even when they were subjected to police violence. “We have done it,” he said, to cries of “victory to India” and “long live the revolution”. But Dipke also emphasised Pradhan’s resignation was “just the beginning” in the movement’s push for systemic education reform and its fight for democratic rights. He also cautioned against people making a hero of him. “Do not make this mistake,” said Dipke. “The country has been ruined by making one person a hero.” Faria Asif, 26, a lawyer who was in the crowd, said: “I am extremely joyous. This is a huge victory, not just for the students, for the constitution and for the entire nation. Being part of this movement has been extremely empowering for all of us. I think it’s the beginning of change.” The news of Pradhan stepping down was met with ecstatic cheers by tens of thousands of CJP supporters gathered in Delhi, who have been demanding accountability from the government. “This is one of the most historic days for our country,” said Rochelle Cope, 27. “For the first time in 12 years, someone from the government has been held accountable for wrongdoing. And it wasn’t political parties that did this; it was the people. “This is a movement of unity, love, solidarity, peace, justice and power. Being here has made me proud to be a citizen of India. This is only the beginning – this government will not be able to rule like it did before.” For many of those present, this week was the first time they had taken part in a political protest and the movement was described as a “gen Z political awakening” in India. Among them was 16-year-old Kanishka Dabla, who said she hoped to become a doctor one day. “It’s wonderful that he has resigned,” she said. “It has made us all feel very powerful. And this also feels like justice for those students who committed suicide because of the exam leaks. It’s made me hopeful for my future again.” In a statement, the CJP said the resignation was a victory for democracy. “We have a free country where we are free to express ourselves, dissent, criticise the government we elect. We will never let anyone take that away from us,” it read. The statement added: “Remember, do not mess with cockroaches.” Sonam Wangchuk, the renowned Indian engineer and activist who had galvanised the movement as he went on a 26-day hunger strike, celebrated the “victory of democracy, straight from the streets”. The CJP demonstrations had taken a dramatic turn on Monday, when hundreds of thousands of young people and students took to the streets of Delhi in the largest youth-led protest seen in years. The police had hit back against the peaceful gatherings with brutality, including teargas and baton charges, leaving hundreds injured. Widespread anger erupted at the violent police response, prompting more people to come out in support of the movement. Throughout this week thousands had flocked to the CJP’s Delhi sit-in to chant slogans against the government and call for Pradhan’s resignation. Demonstrations also broke out across the country, with hundreds of thousands taking to the streets in Kolkata and Mumbai. For weeks, the Modi government had ignored the CJP protesters, but as support grew into ahuge mass movement this week, the government agreed to have a dialogue. Modi had agreed to fast-track justice for the exam leaks, but had made no mention of the CJP’s core demand, the resignation of Pradhan, who was seen as one of his most important and loyal ministers. However, the CJP’s leadership had made it clear the resignation of Pradhan was a non-negotiable demand for the movement. As more protests erupted over the weekend and negotiations were at a deadlock, the BJP government appeared to be backed into a corner. Not all those who took part in the protests were gen Z. Annie Raja, 62, beamed as she looked out at the celebrating protesters. “I feel enthusiastic and happy,” she said. “The young people came out on the streets and they saved our democracy. Previously the government thought they had all the power, and the people were living only in fear. Now the Modi government is scared of us.”

title: Lou Koller, frontman of New York hardcore band Sick of It All, dies aged 59
summary: Keller, who co-founded the celebrated band in 1986, had been battling cancer of the esophagus
body: Lou Koller, the singer and co-founder of New York hardcore band Sick of It All, has died after a battle with cancer, his bandmates announced. Koller was 59. In a social media post on the band’s Instagram page, a statement paid tribute to Koller and his work and said: “The level of loss that we feel at this time is overwhelming.” It added: “We have lost a beloved friend and an iconic frontman. Lou had the power to raise everyone’s spirits at our shows with a smile and a sarcastic comment, and he won people over wherever we played, from every culture and every corner of the world.” Koller revealed in June 2024 that he was suffering from cancer of the esophagus which had extended into his stomach. His illness forced the band to cancel a European tour while he underwent treatment. This year would have seen the band celebrate its 40th anniversary. After intensive treatment, including chemotherapy, Koller was declared cancer-free in May 2025, but the cancer returned shortly after. “His battle is over now and he can finally rest. Hopefully he can somehow still see and feel the beautiful, positive mark he left on the world,” the band’s statement said. Koller was born and raised in Queens, New York. He co-launched Sick of It All with his younger brother and drummer Armand Majidi in 1986 and become a key part of the city’s hardcore music scene. Sick of It All released 12 studio albums and became popular globally through many years of concert touring, winning a passionate audience for their work. • This article was amended on 25 July 2026. Lou Koller’s name was originally misspelled in the headline as Keller.

title: How English-speaking Colombian islands have been caught up in Trump’s ‘drug war’ airstrikes
summary: At least 16 fishers from San Andrés and Providence said to have gone missing since January after US began attacking boats in Caribbean and eastern Pacific
body: Officially, the islands of San Andrés and Providence belong to Colombia – but the language spoken by most of the local Afro-descendant population is not Spanish. Walking among brightly painted wooden houses raised above the ground and lined with verandas – architecture more reminiscent of the Caribbean and the southern US – the language most commonly heard is Creole, a distinct variety of Caribbean English. Yet the same emerald waters that provide fish for local communities and attract tourists from around the world have become “mass graves” for local fishers. Because of the islands’ strategic location north-west of mainland Colombia between South and North America, young seafaring-skilled men have for years been recruited by groups moving cocaine produced in Colombia northwards, often as far as the US. They are members of the Raizal people, shaped by different waves of settlement over the centuries, but above all, defined by their African heritage. Although the involvement of young Raizal men in drug trafficking is not new, residents agree it is growing and has acquired a dramatic dimension since the US began bombing speedboats allegedly carrying drugs in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific. The airstrikes have killed 215 people since September in what the UN has condemned as “extrajudicial killings”. At least 16 fishers from San Andrés and Providence have gone missing since January, according to Edgar Jay Stephens, 58, the president of the main local association of fishers, I-Fish. He said some of them might have been carrying drugs, but “certainly” not all. The disappearances have also been a decades-long problem on the islands – whether because the men were killed, arrested by other countries or fell victim to harsh conditions at sea – but Stephens said the current pace was unprecedented. A spokesperson for US Southern Command, which conducts the airstrikes, said it “does not comment on specific operational details”, but added: “We have no information of any strikes, operations, seizures, or arrests involving residents of San Andrés or Providence.” Given that the US has recently denied responsibility for other bombings in accounts that lawmakers, experts and academics have criticised as inconsistent, Stephens does not rule out the possibility it were involved. “How many people could have died without us knowing what happened to them?” he asked, echoing a frequent criticism made by human rights activists about the bombings: the US does not release information about the victims, making their identification a difficult task that has been accomplished in little more than a dozen cases, thanks mainly to the efforts of lawyers and journalists. The sister of one of the 16 missing men said her brother had been trafficking drugs alongside two other Raizal men. “He accepted the job because it was easy money and he wanted to buy a plot of land and build a house,” said the sister, who asked not to be identified. When she saw the news of a US airstrike on a speedboat carrying three men near Costa Rica, she sent his documents to Colombia’s embassy in the neighbouring country, hoping he might be identified among the three. He was not. Meanwhile, Raizal fishers point to another consequence of the attacks: a direct impact on their livelihoods, as has happened in other traditional communities across the region. “We’ve changed our routines,” said Ling Jay Robinson, 38, explaining that there have been days when he chose not to go out to sea. “Those people [the US military] could mistake us for traffickers and bomb us. We’re living with fear,” said Robinson, who is the son, grandson, great-grandson and great-great-grandson of fishers. “It goes back through our ancestors.” The islands of San Andrés and Providence lie closer to the coast of Nicaragua – 260 miles (420km) away – than to mainland Colombia, which is 450 miles distant. After being initially claimed by Spain, they were permanently settled when English Puritans arrived in 1629. Pirates also passed through, and although Spain later reasserted control, it did not expel the English settlers. Enslaved Africans were subsequently brought to work on plantations, particularly cotton estates. Following Colombia’s independence, the islands agreed to become part of the new nation. But it was only from 1912 onward that the state began to exert significant influence, imposing Catholicism and Spanish as the official religion and language in place of Protestantism and Creole. To this day, however, many Raizales prefer to call Providence by its older name rather than the official Spanish one, Providencia. “I would say that the Raizal people are trilingual. We speak English, Spanish and Creole,” said the political scientist Sally Ann García Taylor, who was born in San Andrés and whose mother is from Providence. The Raizal people, she said, were the product of the interactions between all the peoples who had passed through the islands, although “Afro-descendant heritage is a major element in the formation of our identity”. Another profound change came in 1953, when the government declared San Andrés a freeport – exempting imported goods from taxes – and encouraged large-scale migration from mainland Colombia. The impact is still felt today in the island’s overcrowding. San Andrés, whose airport has daily flights to Bogotá and even Panama, covers 26 sq km (10 sq miles) and is home to 56,000 people. Providence, which has flights only to the neighbouring island, spans 17 sq km and has just 6,000 residents. Many local people say that, with its lack of hotels, fancy restaurants and duty-free shops, it is “like San Andrés 50 years ago”. The difference is also reflected in the islands’ ethnic makeup: while Raizales account for about 91% of Providence’s population, they now make up only 35% of San Andrés’s. The contrast is also visible in the architecture. Providence, although still recovering from Hurricane Iota, which devastated more than 90% of its infrastructure in 2020, has largely preserved its traditional Caribbean architecture, while in San Andrés it is largely confined to the island’s southern areas, where most Raizales live. “If you ask how many Raizales own hotels in San Andrés, I don’t think there are even two or three,” said Jairo Rodriguez Davis, the secretary of the Raizal Council, the community’s main representative and deliberative body, adding that most of the money generated by the island’s tourism industry ended up in the hands of non-Raizales. To determine whether someone is Raizal, he relies on family trees tracing lineages back to the 1700s. “If they have a traceable root back then, you are considered Raizal,” he said. Davis’s office is located in what used to be the first and only Raizal university, created on the initiative of the community and a Baptist minister. The institution operated briefly – teaching in Creole – between the late 1990s and early 2000s, but closed for lack of government and private support. Today the building, stripped of most of its windows, railings and boundary walls, but facing the sea and surrounded by an endless grove of mango trees, serves as a community space for meetings and events. “We dream of having the university here again one day,” said Davis. Davis’s more immediate concern, however, is the violence. “Neither coca is grown here nor cocaine produced here, but many of our young people have been used by traffickers to carry drugs on those boats,” he said. Trafficking has passed through the islands since at least the 1970s: first marijuana heading north, then weapons moving south to fuel Colombia’s armed conflict; later cocaine flowing north again and, more recently, people attempting to reach the US. “Everyone has a relative who has been killed or disappeared at sea,” said Miguel Angel Castell Cano, San Andrés’s government secretary, who previously worked as a lawyer for Providence’s fishers’ association. His own father has been missing for 10 years after becoming involved in a drug-trafficking trip near Honduras. “It is neither something I am ashamed of nor proud of … But no one deserves to disappear, regardless of what they have done,” he said. Being missing does not necessarily mean being dead. Hooker Cabeza Ignacio Agenor, 40, was arrested by Costa Rican authorities in 2021 and sentenced to 10 years in prison for international drug trafficking. He has been eligible to apply for parole since February. His family has submitted a formal repatriation request to the Costa Rican government so that he can serve the remainder of his sentence in Colombia, but they have yet to receive a response. Families are often reluctant to speak out about their missing loved ones. “The islands are deeply religious. When people disappeared, even if they had simply been fishing, no one wants a relative to be subjected to moral judgment,” said the writer and lawyer Maríamatilde Rodríguez. Between the 1990s and 2000s, she led an investigation drawing on documents and interviews with dozens of relatives that arrived at the staggering figure of nearly 700 disappeared people across the two islands over the preceding 30 years. She said updating that count would require a similarly extensive effort. There is no official data from the Colombian authorities about it. “Our sea contains mass graves, and its beauty is matched only by the scale of the tragedies it has witnessed,” she said. Rodríguez said the Colombian state did not treat the issue with the seriousness it deserved. “There is both ignorance and a tendency to minimise the issue – people assume that because the islands are small, the problems must also be small.” The government did not respond to requests for comment. Stephens said that if such a large number of people had gone missing anywhere else in the world, “that would set off alarm bells.
